name: Erythromycin (acne)
lead: Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic that blocks bacterial protein synthesis. [1][2] A 2% topical solution is labelled in the US for the treatment of acne vulgaris. [3]

Acne guidance summarised in a reference encyclopedia describes topical antibiotics, including erythromycin, as typically combined with benzoyl peroxide to limit the development of antibiotic resistance. [1]
infobox: Prescription-only in the US, UK, Australia [2]

paras: The US label for erythromycin topical solution 2% lists acne vulgaris as its indication. [3] Grokipedia describes it as used for mild to moderate inflammatory acne, usually combined with benzoyl peroxide. [1]

The label lists occasional local reactions: peeling, dryness, itching, erythema and oiliness, with eye irritation and skin tenderness also reported. [3] Urticarial reactions requiring steroid treatment have been reported. [3] The label carries a warning about pseudomembranous colitis, which has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents. [3] The label lists pregnancy category B, noting no adequate controlled studies in pregnant women. [3]
Erythromycin binds the 50S bacterial ribosomal subunit and halts protein synthesis; its effect is mainly bacteriostatic. [2][1]

Erythromycin was isolated from a Streptomyces erythreus strain (now Saccharopolyspora erythraea) in soil samples sent from the Philippines by Abelardo Aguilar to Eli Lilly. It launched in 1952 as Ilosone. [2]

timeline.event: Erythromycin launched as Ilosone by Eli Lilly. [2]

card.summary: A prescription macrolide antibiotic solution for acne, usually paired with benzoyl peroxide because acne bacteria can become resistant.
card.note: Often combined with benzoyl peroxide to limit antibiotic resistance.

quick.overview:
Topical erythromycin 2% is a prescription antibiotic labelled in the US for acne vulgaris. Reference sources describe it as a mild-to-moderate acne option, typically combined with benzoyl peroxide.

It is a long-established antibiotic, introduced in 1952.
quick.mechanism: It binds the bacterial ribosome and stops protein synthesis, reducing acne-associated bacteria.
quick.risks: Local dryness, peeling, itching, redness; rare hives. Labels warn of antibiotic-associated colitis. Reference sources note it is usually paired with benzoyl peroxide to limit resistance.
